source: Croskerry (2003) Cognitive forcing strategies in clinical decisionmaking (Ann Emerg Med)
finding: Founding proposal. Cognitive errors cause most ED diagnostic errors. Clinicians use metacognition to build cognitive forcing strategies (CFS) that abort latent errors. Three levels: universal, generic, specific (one per known pitfall).
numbers: No data. A theory and teaching proposal. Abstract only read.
limits: Proposal only, with no test. The abstract claims the method can inoculate trainees; later trials did not show this.
agent_relevance: CFS are rules that fire on a named pitfall. This fits G1 only if the trigger is a detected signal, not a schedule.

source: Ely, Graber, Croskerry (2011) Checklists to reduce diagnostic errors (Acad Med)
finding: Proposes three checklists: general cognitive-approach checklist, differential diagnosis checklist (to avoid not considering the right diagnosis), and a pitfalls and forcing-function list per disease. Authors say they were built informally and never rigorously tested.
numbers: No data. Argument paper. Abstract only read.
limits: Self-declared untested.
agent_relevance: The differential-diagnosis checklist maps to an operator that generates alternatives. Keep it a code-triggered list, not a free prompt.

source: Sherbino, Dore, Siu, Norman (2011) Effectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to decrease diagnostic error: exploratory study (Teach Learn Med)
finding: First experimental look at CFS training. Cross-over design, similar vs novel test cases. Authors conclude application and retention are poor.
numbers: 56 senior medical students on EM rotation; 47 tested at once, 9 tested 2 weeks later; 6 test cases; McNemar test. Abstract gives no effect sizes.
limits: Exploratory, small, students only. Abstract only read. Author list is from memory.
agent_relevance: Training a rule does not guarantee it is applied. A scaffold that applies the rule in code removes the retention problem.

source: Sherbino et al. (2014) Ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to reduce biases in diagnostic reasoning: a controlled trial (CJEM)
finding: CFS training did not reduce errors on search-satisficing or availability cases, nor on false-positive cases. Failed on all four measures.
numbers: n=191 students (145 CFS, 46 control). Second diagnosis search started: 52% vs 48% (p=0.91); correct second diagnosis 54% vs 48% (p=0.13); false-positive second diagnosis 64% vs 77% (p=0.12); availability cases uncommon diagnosis 45% vs 45% (p=0.98).
limits: Novices; students allocated by rotation; 4-week training; computer cases. Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Core negative result for this row: instruction in CFS gave no gain. Do not add a think-about-bias step (section 4b).

source: Norman, Sherbino, Dore et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: controlled trial of System 1 versus System 2 reasoning (Acad Med)
finding: Telling residents to be slow and reflective did not improve accuracy over telling them to be fast. Wrong answers took longer than right ones.
numbers: Residents n=96 (Speed, 2010) and n=108 (Reflect, 2011), 20 computer cases. Accuracy 44.5% vs 45.0% (ns). Time 69 s vs 89 s per case (p<.001). Wrong cases took 17 s longer. Accuracy correlated inversely with time.
limits: Two different years' cohorts, not random assignment; licensing exam scores used to check the cohorts. Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence against slow down as a generic instruction. Supports G1: doubt only on a signal. More time on a case marks it as hard; it does not make the answer right.

source: Norman, Monteiro, Sherbino, Ilgen, Schmidt, Mamede (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking (Acad Med)
finding: Review of the literature. Both Type 1 and Type 2 processes cause errors. Biases can be induced (availability especially) but their share in real errors is not established. Bias-recognition education is ineffective; knowledge reorganisation gives small, steady gains.
numbers: Qualitative review. Quote from abstract.
quote: Educational strategies directed at the recognition of biases are ineffective in reducing errors
limits: Narrative review, not meta-analysis. Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Errors are mostly knowledge errors. A scaffold should invest in retrieval of knowledge and checks against evidence, not bias labels.

source: Graber et al. (2012) Cognitive interventions to reduce diagnostic error: a narrative review (BMJ Qual Saf)
finding: Reviewed 141 articles; 42 tested interventions, 100 only suggested. Three classes: knowledge and experience, reasoning skills (reflective practice, metacognitive review), cognitive help (decision support, second opinions). Most tests used trainees in artificial settings.
numbers: 141 articles reviewed; 42 tested, 100 suggestions, 1 both.
limits: Narrative; tests mostly on trainees. Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: The third class (external cognitive help) is closest to a scaffold. Evidence for it is thin but less bad than for self-awareness training.

source: Lambe, O'Reilly, Kelly, Curristan (2016) Dual-process cognitive interventions to enhance diagnostic reasoning: a systematic review (BMJ Qual Saf)
finding: 28 studies in five groups (education, checklists, CFS, guided reflection, test instructions). Guided reflection was the most consistently successful (five studies). CFS improved accuracy and confidence. Much heterogeneity; mostly early-career doctors. Authors judged the field close to being recommendable.
numbers: 28 studies. No pooled effect size in the abstract.
limits: Systematic review but no pooled effect; heterogeneous outcomes. More positive than Norman 2017, so the evidence is mixed, not zero. Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Guided reflection with structured steps beats generic debiasing. Matches the schema idea of operators that act on the case, not on the thinker.

source: Shimizu, Matsumura, Tokuda (2013) Effects of the use of differential diagnosis checklist and general de-biasing checklist on diagnostic performance (Med Teach)
finding: The differential diagnosis checklist (DDXC) raised scores on difficult cases; the general de-biasing checklist (GDBC) did not. On simple cases the DDXC lowered correct diagnoses.
numbers: 188 students (group 1 n=91, group 2 n=97), 5 cases. Group 1 intuitive 8.25 vs DDXC 8.77 (p=0.01). Group 2 intuitive 7.21 vs DDXC 7.96 (p=0.001). GDBC no gain.
limits: Same students did intuitive first, then checklist, so gain may include simply rethinking. Abstract only read. Author list from memory.
agent_relevance: A content checklist (generate alternatives) helps; a generic de-biasing list does not. Use it only on hard cases, a G1-style gate.

source: Mamede, Schmidt, Penaforte (2008) Effects of reflective practice on the accuracy of medical diagnoses (Med Educ)
finding: Reflective reasoning helped on complex cases but made no difference on simple ones. Pattern recognition was as good on routine cases.
numbers: 42 residents, 16 cases, within-subject. Interaction case complexity x mode F(1,41)=4.48, p<0.05; no main effect of reflection.
limits: Brazilian residents, one site. Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Reflection pays only on hard cases. Gate it on difficulty or disagreement, as G1 says.

source: Sibbald, Sherbino, Ilgen, Zwaan, Blissett, Monteiro, Norman (2019) Debiasing versus knowledge retrieval checklists to reduce diagnostic error in ECG interpretation (Adv Health Sci Educ)
finding: Neither a debiasing checklist nor a knowledge checklist beat control while reading ECGs, even when half the ECGs were engineered to induce bias. Bias cases caused more errors (F=96.9). Possible help for novices.
numbers: 40 PGY-1 residents and 21 cardiology fellows, three arms, 20 ECGs. Both checklists not significantly better than control; no interaction with level.
limits: Single task domain. Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: A bias-aware checklist did not help even when the bias was present by design. A controlled negative result for the checklist idea.

source: Sibbald, de Bruin, Yu, van Merrienboer (2015) Why verifying diagnostic decisions with a checklist can help: insights from eye tracking (Adv Health Sci Educ)
finding: A key-variable checklist at the verification step led residents to fix more errors than a plain silently-check prompt, and eyes covered more of the ECG.
numbers: 16 cardiology residents (PGY 4-6), 12 ECGs (6 per condition, within subject). Errors corrected per ECG: 0.27 vs 0.04 (F(1,15)=8.1, p=.01, eta2=.20). Mean 1.5 errors per ECG (SD 1.4) before checking. Task time 32 vs 21 s; fixations 88 vs 52; leads fixated 65% vs 55%.
limits: Tiny sample; experts only; the checklist is content-specific (rate, rhythm, axis, hypertrophy, ischaemia, intervals), not bias-oriented. The methods text also says 2 ECGs were selected, which does not match 12 checked.
agent_relevance: A checklist of what to verify, applied after an answer, finds errors. It is a G2-like check of real content, not a bias label. Cost: about 50% more time.

source: Chew, Durning, van Merrienboer (2017) Investing in the use of a checklist during differential diagnoses consideration: what is the trade-off? (BMC Med Educ)
finding: A mnemonic checklist (TWED) for gathering more data before closing gave no overall gain on a script concordance test, but did help on the first half of the test; benefit faded under time pressure.
numbers: 88 final-year students, non-equivalent groups, post-test only, 2 weeks after a tutorial. Total median 18.65 vs 18.15 of 30 (U=792, p=0.159). First 5 cases 9.15 vs 8.18 of 15 (p=0.008); last 5 cases 9.58 vs 9.81 (p=0.60). Panel ICC 0.93; Cronbach alpha 0.93.
limits: Not randomised; students; the half split is a post hoc analysis; 30 minute limit.
agent_relevance: Checklist benefit trades against time. A budgeted agent should apply checklists only where budget remains.

source: Japan physicians self-reflection survey (2022) Cognitive Bias and Diagnostic Errors among Physicians in Japan (Int J Environ Res Public Health)
finding: Physicians list anchoring, premature closure and availability as the biases behind their most memorable errors; ED care raised the odds of bias attribution about 4 times.
numbers: 130 of 147 physicians returned forms (88.4%). Mean 3.08 biases per error. Anchoring 60.0%, premature closure 58.5%, availability 46.2%, hassle bias 33.1%. ED odds ratio 3.96 (95% CI 1.16 to 13.6, p=0.028). 43.7% of errors at night; 47.7% in the ED.
limits: Self-report after the fact (hindsight). Bias labels come from the person who erred, so this cannot show that biases cause errors. Authors note limited sampling.
agent_relevance: Shows what clinicians believe causes errors. Useful for a pitfall list, not as proof that debiasing works.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models (npj Digit Med)
finding: BiasMedQA: 1,273 USMLE questions rewritten with seven clinical biases. All six LLMs lost accuracy. Bias education prompts and few-shot examples recovered only part. Some small models broke under few-shot prompts.
numbers: Baseline accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral-8x7B 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama 13B 33.4%. Mean drop: GPT-4 -5.1%, Mixtral -7.7%, GPT-3.5 -17.8%, Llama2 70B -20.1%, PMC-Llama -9.6%. By bias (mean over models): false consensus -24.9%, frequency -18.2%, recency -12.9%, confirmation -8.1%. Bias education gain +3.5 to +6.5% (PMC-Llama -0.1%); GPT-4 frequency +9.3%; GPT-3.5 one-shot +4.3%, few-shot +5.2%; GPT-4 few-shot average 75.2%. PaLM 2 non-response 94.4% (one-shot) and 99.5% (few-shot).
limits: Simple, prompt-injected biases rather than real case bias; gains called modest; top closed models not tested; answer extraction by GPT-3.5 for two models. Figures taken from a page-text summary, not a PDF.
agent_relevance: The only direct LLM test of bias-education prompts in medicine. Gain is small and below the loss. A bias-awareness sentence is weak. False consensus (agreeing with a stated opinion) is the biggest hole, which G4 and G5 already guard against.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster; arXiv 2403.00811)
finding: 13,465 prompts on student admissions test anchoring, framing, group attribution, status quo, primacy. Zero-shot awareness, contrastive and counterfactual prompts gave small and uneven gains; few-shot examples often broke the model (it admitted or rejected nearly all). Letting the model rewrite its own prompt (self-help) worked best for GPT-4.
numbers: GPT-4 framing: admit-rate difference -0.405 baseline, -0.470 with awareness, -0.570 counterfactual, -0.010 self-help. GPT-4 admits 40.5% more in the reject framing. Llama-2-7B judges 32.1% fewer females good at math. Llama models change 40 to 52% of decisions in self-help anchoring. Self-help cut biased prompt elements to 0% (group attribution, GPT-4) and 2.7% (framing, GPT-4). GPT-3.5 self-help cut group attribution only 8.9%.
limits: Admissions task, not medicine. Models: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Llama-2 7B and 13B. Authors discourage using LLMs alone for high-stakes decisions. Table 3 read from PDF text extraction; some columns are ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Awareness prompts can make GPT-4 framing bias worse (-0.405 to -0.470). Rewriting the input to remove the biasing part (a reframe) works better than telling the model about bias. Capacity matters: small models cannot self-debias.

source: Critical Care vignette study (2025) Evaluating the o1 reasoning large language model for cognitive bias (Crit Care); replicates Wang and Redelmeier
finding: Replication and extension of the Wang and Redelmeier ten-vignette test with o1. o1 showed no bias in 7 of 10 vignettes, lower bias than GPT-4 and humans in two, and worse bias in one (Occam's razor, 100% vs 0%). Reasoning models cut bias and noise but are not immune.
numbers: 1,800 responses (90 per version, 10 pairs). Hindsight bias abs diff 52% (o1) vs 85% (GPT-4) vs 56% (humans). Post hoc fallacy 17% vs 56% vs 47%. Occam's razor: 100% vs 0%. Framing 94.4% vs 97.8% (p=0.441). Intra-scenario agreement above 94% in 8 of 10. GPT-4 re-run of 540 responses (framing, primacy, decoy) matched the original Wang results (p<0.001).
limits: Compared with published GPT-4 and human numbers, not same-time controls; one reasoning model; bias is measured as inconsistency across vignette pairs, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Training for step-by-step reasoning cut bias without any debias prompt. Gap-closing cues (a fact that seems to resolve uncertainty) trigger closure. A closure guard could look for such cues in code.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for large language model interpretability in medicine (npj Digit Med)
finding: Prompting an LLM to imitate clinical reasoning styles (intuitive, analytic, differential diagnosis, Bayesian) did not raise accuracy over plain chain of thought. For GPT-3.5 it lowered it. For GPT-4 it was neutral.
numbers: GPT-3.5 MedQA free response: CoT 46%, intuitive 48% (+1.7, p=0.4), analytic 40% (-6.0, p=0.001), differential 38% (-8.9, p<0.001), Bayesian 42% (-4.4, p=0.02). Zero-shot non-CoT 31%. GPT-4 (498 questions): CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, analytic 78%, differential 78%, Bayesian 72% (all ns). NEJM challenge cases GPT-4: CoT 38% vs differential 34% (-4.2, p=0.09). Cohen kappa 0.93 to 0.98.
limits: Small test sets; free-response graded by humans; only OpenAI models.
agent_relevance: A forced differential-diagnosis step did not help GPT-4 and hurt GPT-3.5. Do not add a blanket list-alternatives step; gate it (G1).

source: Griot et al. (2025) Large language models lack essential metacognition for reliable medical reasoning (Nat Commun)
finding: MetaMedQA tests whether models notice what they do not know (missing correct answer, fictional questions). Models rarely say none-of-the-above or I-do-not-know and keep high confidence. Telling the model it may be unable to answer helped most but stayed limited.
numbers: 1,373 questions. GPT-4o 73.3% (SEM 1.2); missing-answer recall 46.1%; GPT-3.5 recall 11.3%. Unknown recall 0% for 9 of 12 models; GPT-4o 3.7%. GPT-4o confidence vs accuracy: high 83.2%, medium 45.9%. Prompts: role-explicit-unknown accuracy 77.4%, unknown recall 44.4%; role-full 78.8%, unknown recall 51.8%; role-omniscient 73.0%.
limits: One benchmark; prompt fixes tested only on GPT-4o; Yi 1.5 9B inflated recall by choosing none 37.9% of the time. Figures from a page-text summary.
agent_relevance: Models do not self-detect missing knowledge, so a debias prompt that asks them to check themselves has no base. Doubt must come from code-detected signals. Explicit permission to abstain helps.

source: Multi-agent bias study (2024) Mitigating cognitive biases in clinical decision-making through multi-agent conversations using LLMs: simulation study (J Med Internet Res)
finding: GPT-4 agents with roles (devil's advocate against confirmation and anchoring bias, facilitator against premature closure, expert, recorder, final decider) corrected a wrong first diagnosis on 16 real misdiagnosis cases. The first responder was wrong in all cases by selection.
numbers: 16 cases x 5 repeats; 80 responses per framework. Initial diagnosis 0/80. Final top-2 differential: framework 3 51/80 (64%), framework 4 55/80 (69%), framework 4-C 61/80 (76%; OR 3.49 vs humans, p=0.002). Humans 13/48 (27%) initial, 23/48 (48%) final.
limits: Cases were chosen because the first diagnosis was wrong, so 0% initial is by design; top-2 scoring; all agents are one model so errors correlate (G4); human comparison group differs.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of a forcing strategy. Roles that argue against the first answer helped, but one model plays both sides, so G4 and G5 apply. A cheaper coded version is one extra pass that does not see the first answer.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: a randomized clinical trial (JAMA Netw Open)
finding: Giving physicians GPT-4 access did not raise diagnostic reasoning scores over usual resources, while GPT-4 alone scored 16 points higher. Physicians did not use it well.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), 60 minutes, up to 6 vignettes. Median score 76% (LLM) vs 74% (control), adjusted diff 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, p=.60). Time 519 vs 565 s (p=.20). LLM alone +16 points (95% CI 2 to 30, p=.03). Trial NCT06157944.
limits: Small; unstructured use of the tool; Nov-Dec 2023 version of GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Human-plus-tool did worse than tool alone. Advice is not used well by clinicians; for our agent, steps decided by code beat steps left to judgment.

source: Qazi, Ali, Khawaja, Akhtar, Sheikh, Alizai (2026) Automation Bias in LLM-Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning among Physicians Trained in AI Literacy (NEJM AI)
finding: Even after 20 hours of AI-literacy training, physicians followed wrong ChatGPT-4o suggestions. Training about bias did not protect against automation bias.
numbers: 44 physicians, 22 per arm, 264 cases. Accuracy 73.3% (erroneous suggestions) vs 84.9% control: -14.0 points (95% CI -18.9 to -9.1, p<0.0001). Top-choice 76.1% vs 90.5%: -18.3 points (95% CI -26.6 to -10.0).
limits: Single trial in Pakistan, June-Aug 2025; abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Awareness training failed again, here for a model's output. Agent side: treat a model's or voter's answer as a hint, not proof (G4).

source: Yan (2026) Independent judgment before viewing generative AI recommendations reduces susceptibility to misleading advice (Front Psychol)
finding: Title reports that forcing an independent judgment before showing AI advice reduces susceptibility to misleading advice. Not opened.
numbers: None read.
limits: Title only; follow up in angle B.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema idea of forming an answer before seeing others' answers (anti-anchoring). Verify before use.

source: Tran, Lee, Patel (2026) AI Timeouts: a structured approach to deliberate AI use in clinician education (J Brown Hosp Med)
finding: Found by search on cognitive forcing; proposes a structured pause before using AI. Not opened. Lead only.
numbers: None read.
limits: Title and index entry only.
agent_relevance: Lead: a forced pause for the human user, similar to a cognitive forcing function.

source: Pham, Illingworth-Vera, Thomas (2026) AI interventions as hypothesis cues: rethinking overreliance in human-AI decision-making (Front Psychol)
finding: Found by search on cognitive forcing; frames AI output as a hypothesis cue rather than advice. Not opened. Lead only.
numbers: None read.
limits: Title and index entry only.
agent_relevance: Lead for later reading on forcing functions for AI users.
